abstract:
Exocytosis of neurotransmitters and peptides begins with the formation of a fusion pore that connects the vesicle lumen to the extracellular space. Release is completed when vesicles undergo full fusion. Here we show that full quanta of serotonin are released through a slowly closing fusion pore without full vesicle fusion. Amperometric recordings of serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in the axons of isolated Retzius neurons of the leech contained a subset of small release currents with a long biexponential decay. These slow-closure currents reflected the release of 90,262 {+/-} 8,829 molecules, a number similar to full-fusion quanta and 54% larger than that of kiss-and-run events. The reconstructed dynamics of fusion pores show that slow-closure pores narrow rapidly after the peak and then close slowly or remain open. By contrast, kiss-and-run pores closed while vesicles still contained a large fraction of their serotonin content. Forces influencing pore kinetics were analyzed from pore velocity. The velocity decay of slow-closure pores developed a rapid undershoot characteristic of near-critical or underdamped relaxation. By contrast, in kiss-and-run pores, velocity decayed exponentially and turned negative during closure, consistent with an overdamped relaxation. Analysis of pore velocity revealed that slow-closure pores initiate rapid closure under a stiff force coupled to the pore diameter. Another force then arrests closure at a residual diameter of 1-2 nm that membrane tension alone cannot sustain. This allows release of the full serotonin quantum.

Impact statementRelease of the entire transmitter content of a vesicle, the quantum, is usually associated with the opening of a fusion pore followed by full vesicle fusion. Here we show that a full serotonin quantum can be released without full fusion, through pores that close rapidly to a residual diameter and then close slowly or stay open.
